rationale: A wins because it keeps four sellable stories cleanly separated without borrowing facts it does not have. Its best line, "Calm built 4 million paying subscribers. Its next 25 million users won't pay it directly," turns the update into a real business-model question with the missing revenue proof named plainly. B is sharper in places, especially "The company that sells the app paid for the study that says the app works," but it gets loose with unsupported backdrop like "demand for care exceeds clinician supply" and starts pitching the skeptical story harder than the founder may be able to survive.
gaps_in_A: The member-use angle, "Free Calm Premium reaches 25 million insurance members — if they actually use it," is good but slightly overlaps the study caveat angle; it needs a clearer member-benefits proof path to avoid becoming a softer rerun of regular-user methodology.
"Decay: week" on the study angle may be generous unless the named journal is strong or the university team is available; A flags proof needs but does not say the angle dies without them.
A could have made the insurer protagonist more explicit. The category angle covers payer decisions, but it misses B's useful question: what did the insurers think they were buying?
gaps_in_B: Invented backdrop: "at a moment when demand for care exceeds clinician supply" is not in the update. B even admits later that no crisis or clinician-supply data was supplied, so this is the draft catching itself after the damage.

Loose reimbursement language: "what insurers agree to reimburse" goes beyond "covered benefit" and "no revenue terms disclosed." If no revenue terms are disclosed, do not smuggle reimbursement into the beat description.

The contrarian angle, "The company that sells the app paid for the study that says the app works," is journalistically strong but strategically dangerous; B names the liability, then still elevates it as a core pitch shape without enough gating.

Business-model overreach: "routing around app-store retail" and "whether B2C consumer wellness has stopped growing" are plausible questions, not supplied facts. They need to stay framed as questions, not narrative scaffolding.
